name: Vanishing White Matter Disease
aliases: Childhood Ataxia with Central Nervous System Hypomyelination

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Vanishing White Matter Disease Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Progressive neurological deterioration with stress or febrile illness triggering episodes
Characteristic MRI showing diffuse cerebral white matter rarefaction and cystic degeneration
Biallelic pathogenic variants in any of the EIF2B1-5 genes
Onset typically in infancy or early childhood but can be variable
Lack of inflammatory markers in CSF and brain biopsy

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of progressive neurological symptoms triggered by stress, characteristic MRI findings, and confirmation by genetic testing
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing; MRI findings are highly suggestive but not pathognomonic alone.

pathognomonic.notes: Neurological worsening triggered by fever, minor head trauma, or acute stress

pathognomonic.symptomName: Diffuse cerebral white matter rarefaction on MRI

laboratory: Normal cerebrospinal fluid without inflammatory markers
Elevated lactate may be absent or mild
imaging: MRI showing diffuse rarefaction and cystic degeneration of cerebral white matter
Progressive disappearance of cerebral white matter signal on T2-weighted images
genetic: Biallelic mutations in EIF2B1, EIF2B2, EIF2B3, EIF2B4, or EIF2B5 genes
other: Stress or fever precipitates rapid neurological decline
Absence of significant inflammatory or infectious findings

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of Rosenthal fibers on biopsy
Predominant frontal white matter involvement on MRI
Elevated N-acetylaspartic acid in urine and brain

redFlags: Rapid neurological deterioration following febrile illness or minor head trauma
Early onset progressive ataxia with spasticity
Characteristic MRI showing cystic degeneration of cerebral white matter
references: van der Knaap MS, et al. Vanishing white matter disease: a review. J Child Neurol. 2006.
Bugiani M, et al. Vanishing white matter disease: a leukodystrophy due to astrocytic dysfunction. Brain. 2010.
Leegwater PA, et al. Mutations in eIF2B cause vanishing white matter disease. Nat Genet. 2001.
